name: Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia
summary: A persistently saturated or directly measured oxygen-limited root zone can suppress Cannabis root elongation, leaf expansion, relative chlorophyll, gas exchange, and biomass. Above-ground responses overlap drought, nutrient, transplant, viroid, and root-disease injury; measured exposure, serial root context, and pathogen exclusions are required.
affectedParts: active root tips and fine-root system
root crown and lower stem as disease-exclusion tissue
whole canopy and total leaf area
expanding and mature fan leaves tracked by canopy position
indicators: Root zone remains saturated or stands in water across repeated observations
Irrigation input, container mass, drainage time, or calibrated substrate-water measurements document inadequate dryback rather than inferred overwatering
Dissolved oxygen is low in a liquid root zone when measured with a calibrated method, while recognizing that saturation and hypoxia are related but not interchangeable labels
Whole-plant growth and canopy expansion slow relative to a matched healthy plant
Root system is shorter or produces fewer visibly active new tips than a matched control
Relative canopy greenness declines gradually without a lesion-defined pattern
Leaf-area development, gas exchange, or chlorophyll-fluorescence measurements decline during the documented exposure
Root, leaf-area, or biomass growth remains depressed during a documented short recovery after drainage is restored
exclusions: Container weight or representative substrate-water measurement shows the root zone is dry rather than saturated
High vapor demand, irrigation interruption, emitter failure, or another measured water-shortage event explains the wilt or reduced growth
The pattern is restricted to one mechanically damaged branch or one locally obstructed root zone
Discrete leaf lesions, fungal growth, vascular discoloration, root galls, insects, or other organisms provide a better causal explanation
Roots are brown, soft, necrotic, or decayed and laboratory testing identifies Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or another pathogen
Measured salinity, unsuitable pH, or root-zone temperature is sufficient to explain the distribution and timing
Container binding, transplant injury, compacted media, or poor initial rooting explains limited root development without a documented saturation history
Only canopy posture, yellowing, or one photograph is available without irrigation, drainage, root, and time-series context

progression.description: Before attributing symptoms, document normal irrigation input, container mass or substrate water content, drainage, root appearance, pH, EC, temperature, and oxygen where the production system supports direct measurement.

The container, bed, or solution root zone remains saturated, flooded, poorly drained, or directly oxygen limited across time. Canopy appearance may still be nonspecific, so the sample remains an exposure-linked observation rather than a confirmed causal image label.

In Cannabis cv. G1, seven days of controlled waterlogging reduced root length, leaf area, leaf-area index, relative chlorophyll, stomatal conductance, and plant biomass compared with the study controls.

In the same experiment, root length, leaf area, and biomass remained depressed after seven recovery days. New root-tip production and new canopy expansion are more informative than expecting old pale or damaged tissue to recover.

Longer study exposure reduced leaf-area index, relative chlorophyll, photosynthetic efficiency, root and shoot biomass, and flower biomass; the magnitude varied with stage and duration and is not a universal visual timeline.

lookAlikes: Excessive vapor demand or acute canopy dehydration
Fusarium wilt, crown rot, or root rot
Rhizoctonia sore shin or root rot
Rice root aphid or fungus-gnat larval root injury
Root binding, compaction, transplant damage, or poor clone establishment
High root-zone EC or broad salinity stress
Acidic, alkaline, or otherwise unsuitable root-zone pH
Nitrogen deficiency or normal late-cycle senescence
Hop latent viroid or another systemic decline syndrome
confirmation: Do not confirm overwatering, waterlogging, or root-zone hypoxia from droop, yellowing, brown roots, slow growth, one photograph, or one video.

Document irrigation volume and timing, shot size and frequency, drainage duration, runoff, standing water, container mass, and calibrated substrate-water content across multiple wetting and dryback cycles.

Capture serial whole-plant, upper/middle/lower-canopy, leaf-surface, container, drain, root-crown, and cleaned-root views with scale, neutral lighting, leaf age, and a matched healthy same-cultivar control.

Measure root-zone temperature, pH, and EC; in hydroponic or liquid systems, record dissolved oxygen with a calibrated method and sampling location rather than inferring hypoxia from water presence alone.
Compare root length, fine-root density, visibly active root tips, leaf-area expansion, and new growth during exposure and after drainage correction; old damaged tissue is not a recovery endpoint.

When roots or crowns are discolored, soft, necrotic, decayed, or malodorous, submit linked root, crown, and water samples to a plant diagnostic laboratory for Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, and other plausible organisms before assigning an abiotic-only label.

Inspect for root aphids, fungus-gnat larvae, galls, binding, compaction, and transplant damage, and consider HLVd testing when poor root development and systemic stunting persist without a measured saturation-response link.
immediateActions: Stop adding unnecessary irrigation and remove standing water while preserving a documented sample of the pre-correction root-zone condition.
Separate drainage and runoff from healthy plants when infectious root disease remains possible.
Inspect roots, emitters, drain paths, and neighboring containers before choosing a correction.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured cause of persistent saturation, such as blocked drainage, excessive shot size or frequency, poor container drainage, compacted media, or flooding.
Return irrigation gradually to a measured dryback pattern appropriate to the crop stage and medium, then score only new growth and root recovery.
Use laboratory results and locally legal crop protocols if a root pathogen is confirmed; drainage correction alone does not establish or cure a pathogen diagnosis.
prevention: Record irrigation input, runoff, container weight or substrate water content, and dryback duration instead of relying on a fixed calendar.
Use matched healthy controls and photograph the whole plant, root zone, and cleaned roots across time.
Keep drainage paths functional and prevent shared runoff from moving between containers.
warnings: Reduced growth, pale foliage, droop, leaf angle, or canopy recovery after drainage is not specific to excess water and must not be used as image-only ground truth.
Saturation, waterlogging, and low dissolved oxygen are related observations but are not interchangeable unless the relevant exposure was measured in the photographed plant.

The controlled waterlogging results come from one Cannabis genotype and defined seven-to-21-day treatments; symptom timing, root length, physiology, and severity should not be generalized as universal thresholds.
Brown or decayed roots can occur with excessive water and with Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, and other diseases; morphology alone cannot establish an abiotic cause.
Excess water can both injure roots and favor or spread root pathogens, so drainage correction does not retrospectively prove that the original syndrome was pathogen-free.
The greenhouse pathogen source is a management review, not an abiotic waterlogging trial; it supports differentials and measurement safeguards rather than a positive visual hypoxia class.

No symptom photograph or video with plant-linked Cannabis saturation or oxygen measurements, laboratory pathogen exclusions, serial progression, and reusable item-level rights was admitted; media remain empty rather than using anecdotal, vendor, forum, or generated imagery.
All symptom-only, root-unlinked, measurement-free, single-timepoint, or disease-confounded samples require human review.

sources.title: Impact of varying water stress periods (water shortage vs. waterlogging) on Cannabis sativa growth, leaf physiology, and CBD content
sources.publisher: University of Agricultural Sciences and Veterinary Medicine Cluj-Napoca
supportedClaims: In a controlled Cannabis sativa cv. G1 experiment, waterlogging was imposed by standing potted plants in a two-centimetre sheet of water; diagnosis therefore depended on verified root-zone exposure rather than canopy appearance alone.

After seven vegetative-stage days, waterlogged plants had shorter roots, lower leaf area, lower leaf-area index, lower chlorophyll-meter readings, and less biomass than controls; their growth remained lowest after a seven-day recovery period.

During reproductive-stage exposure, waterlogging reduced leaf-area index, root and shoot biomass, stomatal conductance, relative chlorophyll content, and photosystem-II efficiency as duration increased, but responses varied with stage and duration.

Water shortage produced overlapping reductions in several above-ground measurements, so reduced canopy growth or greenness cannot distinguish excess water from insufficient water without root-zone measurements.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A 2017–2018 North Carolina survey based on 572 agronomic and 117 plant-clinic hemp submissions attributed common environmental disorders to excessive rainfall flooding roots and to poor root development in transplanted clones.
The same diagnostic survey found Pythium diseases in greenhouse hemp, supporting explicit separation of abiotic flooding injury from root-pathogen diagnoses.

sources.title: Integrated Management of Pathogens and Microbes in Cannabis sativa L. (Cannabis) under Greenhouse Conditions
supportedClaims: In greenhouse Cannabis, root browning can occur with Fusarium or Pythium infection and with excessive waterlogging, so brown roots do not distinguish an abiotic oxygen problem from infectious root disease.

The review links Cannabis root-pathogen syndromes with yellowing, stunting, reduced root development, and plant death, and states that excessive watering or flooding can exacerbate infection and spread inoculum.
For recirculating production, the authors recommend monitoring water temperature and oxygen as well as pH, EC, and drip-to-drain nutrient relationships because extremes can enhance root infection.
Fusarium and Pythium inoculum may occur in recirculated Cannabis nutrient solutions; pathogen testing is therefore required when root discoloration or decline remains compatible with disease.

The article is a greenhouse-disease management review rather than a controlled abiotic-waterlogging trial, so its root-browning and monitoring statements support differential diagnosis and exclusion checks, not an image-only hypoxia label.
